newsitem.title: USA: Andrew Lloyd Webber show to debut in Washington.
newsitem.headline: Andrew Lloyd Webber show to debut in Washington.

text.p: Britain's Andrew Lloyd Webber, creator of theatrical hits, was overseeing final preparations on Friday for the world premiere of "Whistle Down the Wind," a Cajun-flavored musical featuring gospel and rock.

Smaller in scale than his previous productions such as "Phantom of the Opera" and "Sunset Boulevard" and devoid of big names, "Whistle" opens for previews on Dec. 6 at the National Theatre, a few blocks from the White House. The Broadway opening is scheduled for April 17.

Why Washington? "'Whistle Down the Wind' is an American story and it's appropriate that it opens here first," Lloyd Webber said in a statement when the premiere was announced last summer. It will be the first world opening of one of his shows outside England since "Jesus Christ Superstar" bowed on Broadway in 1971.

This version of the story, set in Louisiana in 1959, may be American, but it is based on a 1960s-era novel and movie set in the north of England in which three children shelter a stranger in their barn, believing he is Jesus Christ. The Louisiana bayou setting allowed Lloyd Webber to draw on the musical influences of gospel and early rock 'n' roll.
A spokesman for the show, John Wimbs, said promotion for the Washington debut was being kept local and low-key.

"This is a pre-Broadway engagement and we're not creating a lot of focus on it ... so that all the creators can have one look at it before bringing the show to New York City in the spring," Wimbs said by telephone.

While theatregoers have flocked to Lloyd Webber's productions, the New York critics have often been caustic, especially Frank Rich of The New York Times, who so bedevilled the playwright that he once bought a gelded racehorse and named it for the powerful critic.
Rich, now a columnist, has already taken aim at "Whistle," grouping it with what he described as "musical theme-park rides" such as "Phantom of the Opera," "Miss Saigon" and "Sunset Boulevard."

Rich wrote on Nov. 20 that three home-grown productions -- "Rent," "Bring In da Noise, Bring In da Funk" and a revival of Bob Fosse's "Chicago" -- "are rapidly bringing the era of the British megamusical to an end,"

Thanks to the Internet, Lloyd Webber fans can check out the cast and see a list of songs for "Whistle" by consulting several pages on the World Wide Web, including http://www.serve.com/dougmac/ and http://www.reallyuseful.com/.
